To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the frequency of occurrence of fragments in a fingerprint can be used to weight the contributions of fragments to similarity, that the square root of fragment frequencies is the best choice of weighting scheme, that the use of frequency-based similarity measures can significantly improve the performance of similarity-based virtual screening systems, and that the use of a frequency-based similarity measure with a standardised weighting scheme is the best way to use fragment occurrence data for virtual screening.

the use of fragment- occurrence weights is generally more effective in similarity-based virtual screens than unweighted screening, and that standardizing the raw frequencies by taking the root of the occurrence frequencies will maximise effectiveness.

frequency-based weighting of fragment occurrence data can be used to improve the performance of similarity-based virtual screening, but that the effectiveness of the weighting depends on the fingerprint used and on the similarity coefficient used in the screening process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of fragment-ocurrence data in similarity based virtual screening.
the development of new methods for similarity-based virtual screens, and with the use of fragment- and substructure-based similarity coefficients to improve the effectiveness of virtual screens.
the development of new methods for the analysis of fragment-occurence data in virtual screening and the development of new similarity measures based on this data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
frequency-based weighting is the most effective method of similarity-based screening.
the best weighting scheme is that in which the frequencies of occurrence of the fragments in the fingerprint are normalised to the square root of their frequencies.
, in the absence of any other knowledge, frequency-based screening is the most effective way to perform virtual screening.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
frequency-weighted screening, using the appropriate similarity coefficients, can improve virtual screening performance by 10-20% over unweighted screening.
the best fingerprint for virtual screening depends on the database of compounds to be searched.
frequency-based similarity screening, using the Pipeline Pilot ECFC fingerprint with the Euclidean coefficient and square-root weighting, is a highly effective method of virtual screening.
The main takeaway from our work is that

fragment-based weighting is an important factor in virtual screening, and that the use of fragment-based similarity measures is a viable and effective alternative to the use of more complex similarity measures.
, when using fingerprints to calculate similarity, one should always consider weighting the fragments by their frequency of occurrence in molecules.
the use of frequency-based weighting in similarity measures can improve the performance of virtual-screening systems, and this can be achieved by using a simple and straightforward method.
